rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage reinforces its opening call to obey God and His Messenger by recalling divine favours, eliciting gratitude and service, and assuring believers of continued help rather than fear.
rows.anchor: All these favours entail that they show gratitude to God and become useful members of His religion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 8:27 parallels 8:24: the positive directive there is restated here by forbidding its opposite.
rows.anchor: This verse is in exact parallel to the directive which is mentioned in verse 24.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gratitude means recognizing God's right, acknowledging it, and fulfilling it sincerely.
rows.anchor: the real essence of gratitude is to recognize the right of God, to acknowledge it and to fulfil it with sincerity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After pledging obedience, believers must remain sincere to God and His Messenger; every promise is a trust, and breaking it openly or secretly is dishonesty.
rows.anchor: He should always fulfil this promise because every promise is a trust and it is dishonesty to breach it, whether openly or secretly.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As in 2:42, the un-repeated negation signals a natural consequence: insincerity toward God and His Messenger opens the way to betraying people's responsibilities and trusts.
rows.anchor: if the particle of negation is not repeated, it is an indication that hiding of the truth is a natural consequence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amānat has a broad Qur'anic sense, encompassing rights and responsibilities arising from covenants or naturally, as well as human capacities and favours; these must not be deliberately betrayed.
rows.anchor: in verse 58 of S ūrah al-Nisā’ that it is mentioned in the Qur’ ān in a very broad meaning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qualifier “deliberately” is a reprimand aimed at the people addressed.
rows.anchor: The condition “deliberately” is meant to reprimand people who are referred to here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the sūrah's address appears general, Islahi says it is directed particularly to the group of weak Muslims.
rows.anchor: though the apparently the address in the whole of this sūrah is general, yet it is directed towards the group of weak Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context makes the opening “be informed” mark the directive as weighty and certain.
rows.anchor: The context in which the words “and be informed” occur shows the grand as well as the certain nature of the directive stated here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After inappropriate questions about spoils and a discussion of the questioners' weakness, this verse gives the detailed answer as an admonition to hear and obey carefully, without hesitation, because it comes from the sovereign of the universe.
rows.anchor: some people had raised some very inappropriate questions about the spoils of war.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ghanima means to acquire something without paying an exchange; ghanīmah names things and resources Muslims capture from disbelievers on the battlefield.
rows.anchor: to acquire something without exchange for anything.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling captured property nafal and ghanīmah shows that spoils are extra gains, not war wages: fighting for God fulfills a duty whose reward is in the afterlife, so soldiers should not covet spoils.
rows.anchor: this is not a remuneration for the war waged. It is just a secondary benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jāhiliyyah treated spoils as war's true benefit and measured success by them; some weak Muslims adopted this view at Badr, and the Qur'an reforms it.
rows.anchor: Some weak Muslims too were influenced by this concept and this showed itself in the battle of Badr.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The allocation in this verse is the detailed answer to the question in the sūrah's opening verse: spoils are collectively owned, after an initial brief answer and a discourse reforming the group's mentality.
rows.anchor: form the detailed answer to the question raised in the very first verse of the sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In jāhiliyyah, chiefs personally took a quarter of plunder, called mirbā‘; Islam assigns a fifth to God and the Messenger for society's welfare.
rows.anchor: the chiefs took one-fourth of the plundered wealth. It was called mirbā‘.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needs nothing; His share is set aside to make His word prevail, protect, promote, and defend it, with the means varying by time and society but the purpose unchanged.
rows.anchor: His share is actually reserved to make His word prevail, to safeguard it and to promote and defend it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi tentatively assigns the Messenger's share to his Madīnah head-of-state office: God undertook Muhammad's needs as envoy, while public service warranted a personal-use provision that passes to later rulers.
rows.anchor: I am inclined to think that this is not mentioned in his individual capacity but in his capacity of head of state.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The near relatives are those dependent on the Prophet for livelihood and whose needs he considered his responsibility, including poor, needy, or handicapped family members under ethical, religious, or customary obligations.
rows.anchor: by these are meant those relatives who were dependent on the Prophet (sws) for their livelihood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relatives' share continues after the Prophet's death; otherwise it would not have been listed independently.
rows.anchor: this share must continue even after the Prophet (sws) passes away otherwise it would not have been mentioned independently.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām attached to the first three shares is omitted for the poor, orphans, and wayfarers because their share is nested under the relatives' share, honoring them as if they were the Prophet's kin.
rows.anchor: This fourth category of shares is actually mentioned under the third stated share of near relatives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Orphans and the needy belong to the head of state's family in status; the ruler should care for them at least as much as for his own household.
rows.anchor: the status of the orphans and the needy is of the family of the head of state.

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: The caliph ʿUmar reportedly said that his state share should be only what an orphan's guardian may take from the orphans' property, and that the state's needy and wayfarers were directly his responsibility.
rows.anchor: ‘Umar (rta) is reported to have said that his share in the wealth of the state is only as much as that of a guardian

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A society that neglects orphans, leaves the needy hungry, and fails to care for wayfarers has no genuine connection to Islam, whatever it claims.
rows.anchor: can have no link with Islam whatever claim it may make.

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some interpreters take lām as indicating personal ownership and therefore bar spending this share on collective welfare projects; Islahi says this view has little linguistic weight.
rows.anchor: there are people who regard the particle ل (lām) to be that of tamlīk (personal possession)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because lām can mean benefit as well as personal possession, an Islamic government may spend this share on collective relief; individual payments are not always required.
rows.anchor: One of these meanings is to provide benefit.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawm al-furqān is the day of Badr; the following phrase about the two groups meeting explains the name, since it was the first battle between believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: refers to the day in which the battle of Badr was fought.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh leaders treated Badr as a test of success, asserting that its loser would be deviant and its winner would adhere to truth.
rows.anchor: The leaders of the Quraysh themselves had regarded this battle to be a barometer of success.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's help at Badr was manifested so clearly and in so many ways that everyone could tell which side God supported; the revelation phrase points to this aid.
rows.anchor: everyone could clearly discern on whose side God was.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing condition reinforces the allocation directive: believers should distribute spoils without hesitation if they believe in God and His decisive help at Badr, where truth met falsehood.
rows.anchor: they should follow the directive of distributing the spoils without any hesitancy
